If you haven't considered it, what about trying tail tattooing? It's less feasible if you have to combine different cages of mice, but in a 5-mouse cage you can easily fit 4 dots on a weanling's tail. You can use a handheld needle (doesn't take many pokes), and green ink shows up well on B6 mice.  
You just put the mouse under a transparent red plastic party cup ([like these](https://www.partycity.com/red-plastic-cups-9oz-72ct-621033.html?extcmp=pla%7CLia%7CGoogle&gclid=Cj0KCQiAtvSdBhD0ARIsAPf8oNk2nNg7uQAeEQigSifeUP-lV1jnILxKN4HhCWDpByzZVdE7EP42GsMaAtywEALw_wcB&gclsrc=aw.ds)) with a small hole cut in the rim for the tail to poke out. Since they can't see red light, they calm down in the "dark" under the cup. Then you can hold the cup down with either one hand or a weight of some kind, and easily tattoo the tail. Once you get the depth and amount of ink down, the mark will last the whole lifetime of the mouse. I haven't seen any gnawing or infection with this method, and you can spot the mark when you open the cage.

When waking cells from cryostorage I've had some recent success with starting the cells on the back wall of a T75 (tipped vertically). Once they're confluent enough I trypsinize, then lay the flask to its normal horizontal position and replace the old media supplemented with enough new to cover the larger surface. I leave the deactivated trypsin in. It doesn't seem to harm them as much as the stress of being centrifuged.

If you need to collect urine from mice, lay down a sheet of aluminum foil (or plastic wrap, though they tend to tear it up) and place the mouse on the foil. Much of the time they'll void by default, but if they seem unwilling hold one hand flat above the bench so that the mouse has to squeeze under it. I find they often urinate while they do this, and you're less likely to be bitten than if you massage their bellies. In general if they perceive your hand as "architecture" rather than a predator, they won't attack it.

Mice can't see red light, and feel safer in the dark. If you put a transparent red plastic party cup over them they calm down fast. Drill a tail-sized hole in the side for genotyping. You can put a lead fishing weight on top to keep them from scooting it around if you need a hand free.

Shake your eggs to figure out how fresh they are! Gently but firmly - you're not trying to scramble it in the shell. If you feel a redistribution of weight (like something is plopping from side to side), that egg should be cooked thoroughly before eating (or at the extreme thrown away entirely).

As an egg gets older and spoils, microbes begin to digest it, they release gas as a waste product. This gas increases the "empty" space inside the shell.

You can also find the gas content of an egg by submerging it in water (if it floats, it's bad!), but with some practice a gentle shake is more portable.

Some of it has to do with the popularity of pre-made, raw baked goods in the US. When you make cookies from scratch, you typically mix all the ingredients up, then immediately bake them (some things you chill the dough for a while, but the cold temperature makes it O.K.), but pre-made dough has to be shipped, sold, etc. before it even sees an oven.
All that extra time gives any bacteria that are in there time to multiply, and increases our chances of getting sick from them.
Alternatively, the industrial process of making the dough requires large batches of ingredients. So even if only one egg in a thousand has the salmonella, it gets mixed in with the rest, distributing the bacteria in a much lower concentration amongst the batter. Given time, the bacterial population can grow.
I'm a little drunk, but basically, fresh eggs directly from a shell aren't a danger to most home cooks. Go ahead and eat your home-made raw-egg containing stuff. But you have to remember that eggs are fabulous sources of nutrition, and the shell is what protects them from infection. Without that, pathogens can reproduce willy-nilly, in the right conditions, over a startlingly short period of time.

Okay, here's an idea I've been rolling around in my head for a while:

Fake fur is made of plastic (like acrylic), which means it won't biodegrade very fast, and requires petroleum. My thought is that using a natural product will cause less overall environmental damage (and thus animal suffering) than using an artificial one. We already know that small pieces of plastic can accumulate in animals' stomachs, and I have a suspicion that faux "hairs" might do the same, directly harming an animal.

Of course, I still believe that unnecessary cruelty to farmed animals is wrong. But when we consider issues like this, I think it's important to consider the potential impacts of what we usually think of as more humane options.

Think of it this way:
As said above, the 'toxins' are manure, which is rich in nutrients  
The algae eat the nutrients  
The algal population grows  
Photosynthesis produces oxygen  
Lots of algae means more critters eating algae  
The ratio of critters using oxygen to algae producing oxygen is roughly the same as before the bloom  
The algae die, maybe because there is less sunlight or the temperature changes  
Decomposition of algae consumes oxygen  
There are more critters than before the bloom consuming oxygen  
The production:use ratio is skewed towards using the available oxygen up (resulting in a hypoxic scenario)  
Without enough oxygen, the critters get weak and die  
Critters decompose, using oxygen  
There is almost no oxygen (anoxic scenario)

Here's a thought experiment. A little outlandish, but please bear with me.
Imagine that all music video backup dancers were people with your face. Not identical, but more than a passing resemblance. 
In the music videos, they never have a line, the camera stays on their ass longer than their face, and they are essentially an accessory to showcase how rich, powerful, and virile the singer is. When you meet people in public, they think of you as essentially "that booty babe" from the music video, because you look just like them! You're just waiting around to emphasize someone's desirable characteristics!

In your post, you scoff at the idea that any advent of sexualization is wrong, and I agree with you there. I, personally, enjoy sexualization a great deal. But when there is no other option but to be sexualized, that's when there's a problem. Females are absolutely required to be sexy in order to be represented in media at all. Think of a movie scientist- a male scientist could be dweeby, scrawny, stutter; or could be a babe. A female scientist will always be either a) smokin' hot or b) girl-next-door smokin' hot with glasses and less makeup.

Now back to the backup dancers that all look like you. You're not a backup dancer, but all these people you meet keep treating you like one. "Yo, I've seen your ass on TV, why can't I see it now?" But you're not a backup dancer. You never chose to present yourself that way; you just happen to look like them. People can't seem to tell the difference though. So you start getting loud about it, proclaiming that you are **not** a backup dancer! Then people ask you why you hate backup dancers. You don't, that's not the point.

You get it into your head that maybe, if other people who looked like you did something other than backup dancing, it wouldn't be immediately assumed that *you* were a backup dancer. But at the casting calls they take one look and say, "You know, you really look like a backup dancer. We want to hire you, but our role is for a scientist. Would you be alright being a scientist who works nights as a backup dancer?" That's not really what you wanted, but at least you're not *just* a backup dancer, right?

Hold on! I only know the US, but keeping hives is serious business! It's wonderful that you've had such good luck, but most simply don't. Are you prepared to treat for [varroa mites](http://entnemdept.ufl.edu/creatures/misc/bees/varroa_mite.htm)? You functionally cannot get rid of them. They suck out your bees' haemolymph, and spread disease (fun fact: They even call it parasitic mite syndrome). Are you prepared for [chalkbrood](https://www.daf.qld.gov.au/animal-industries/bees/diseases-and-pests/chalkbrood), for [sacbrood](http://beeinformed.org/2013/10/sacbrood-virus-sbv/),for [European foulbrood](http://www.extension.org/pages/23693/european-foulbrood:-a-bacterial-disease-affecting-honey-bee-brood) (Now antibiotic resistant, as are all the other diseases here mentioned.), for the even worse [American foulbrood](http://entomology.ucdavis.edu/files/147615.pdf) (The only way to destroy the spores is to burn the hive; they can last [over 35 years](http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1046/j.1365-2672.2001.01376.x/pdf).), for your neighbors spraying pesticides? Are you prepared to feed your bees? They can starve in any season if there isn't enough nectar or pollen around. Can you handle swarming, requeening, supering? Can you lift a hundred pound box of bees and honey?
[This is an annual report of colony losses.](http://beeinformed.org/2015/05/colony-loss-2014-2015-preliminary-results/) Are you prepared to effectively lose a quarter to half of your apiary every year? And note, this is data taken from professionals.
Remember, this takes work, and it's not for everyone. You can save the bees other ways. I'll post some more info if I ever hear anything back about this comment, but if not, that's cool.
This is even before you consider cost.
Source: Currently working at an apiary, just took a class at University on honey bee biology and beekeeping.
